questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of linear search?

answer.text: Scan elements one by one from the start, comparing each with the target until a match is found or the end is reached

feedback.text: Correct — a sequential scan of every element in order.

answer.text: Repeatedly halve the search interval by comparing the middle element

feedback.text: That is binary search, which needs a sorted array.

answer.text: Estimate the probe position from the target's value

feedback.text: That is interpolation search.

answer.text: Split the range using Fibonacci numbers

feedback.text: That is Fibonacci search.

generalfeedback.text: Linear (sequential) search simply walks through the collection comparing each element to the target.

questiontext.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search over n elements?

feedback.text: Correct — in the worst case every element must be examined.
That requires a sorted array and halving (binary search).
That is the best case, when the target is the first element.
Too large; a single scan is O(n).

generalfeedback.text: The target may be absent or last, forcing a full scan, so the worst case is O(n).

questiontext.text: What is the best-case time complexity of linear search?

feedback.text: Correct — the target is found at the very first position.
That is the worst case, not the best.
Linear search does not halve the range.
That is interpolation search's average on uniform data.

generalfeedback.text: If the first element checked is the target, the search finishes in constant time.

questiontext.text: What ordering precondition does linear search require on its input?

answer.text: None — it works on unsorted data

feedback.text: Correct — linear search makes no assumption about ordering.

answer.text: The array must be sorted in ascending order

feedback.text: No — that is required by binary and Fibonacci search, not linear search.

answer.text: The values must be uniformly distributed

feedback.text: No — that helps interpolation search, not linear search.

answer.text: The array must support O(1) random access

feedback.text: No — linear search works even on linked lists with only sequential access.

generalfeedback.text: Because it just walks through elements, linear search needs no sorting or random access — it is the only option for unsorted or linked data without extra structure.

questiontext.text: Which statements about linear search are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It works on unsorted data with no ordering precondition

feedback.text: Yes — no sorting is needed.

answer.text: It can search a singly linked list, which lacks O(1) random access

feedback.text: Yes — sequential access is enough.

answer.text: It runs in O(log n) time in the worst case

feedback.text: No — its worst case is O(n).

answer.text: It requires the array to be sorted first

feedback.text: No — linear search has no sorting precondition.

generalfeedback.text: Linear search: O(n) worst case, no ordering requirement, works on unsorted and linked data.

questiontext.text: Linear search requires the array to be sorted before it can run.

feedback.text: No — linear search works on unsorted data.
Correct — no ordering precondition is needed.

questiontext.text: Linear search uses only O(1) extra (auxiliary) space.

feedback.text: Correct — it needs only a constant number of variables.
Linear search keeps just an index, so its extra space is O(1).

questiontext.text: Because its running time grows in direct proportion to n, linear search is said to run in ______ time. Give the one-word adjective.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct — linear time is O(n).
